messages.content: OK, just one question: how was the experiment?

I really enjoyed it. I felt frustrated with myself at times because of the pressure to find words from the back of my mind, but I found it enjoyable. The process of creating words during the smart lab experiment was interesting, especially finding a rhythm behind it.
When you say finding a rhythm...
Yeah.
Do you mind telling me a bit more about the rhythm?
Mm.
More about the rhythm.

From my understanding, it felt like constructing my own rules. With the way the words came through, I began to associate certain words with others towards the bottom. If a word came through that felt like it could be phrased as an opinionated phrase, I would assign it that way. When that changed, I'd start putting together a different word to associate with opinion or attitude. I felt a moment when the rules kind of flipped, and I'd try to associate the new phrase as I went along, until it felt like I had self-constructed my own ruleset for that particular experiment.
That's really interesting.
That's how it felt, anyway.
Yeah. At what point in the experiment did that happen?

Probably within the first five to ten words that came through. As soon as it changed from being attitude, opinion, or something else—as soon as the word 'edge' or 'considerations' started to change—for some reason it just worked in my head that I could put 'edge' and associate that with consideration, and another word could be associated with opinion. It just became interchanging those words.
That's really interesting. What was your ruleset like? If you had to describe it—which I know is a very unfair question—did it feel a certain way?

Yeah. Think of it like this: you'd have a word you could associate with the top word. If you had something like 'salty' and 'sour' and the options were 'edge' or 'opinion', I'd have clicked on 'opinion' before. But if it came with 'consideration' and 'edge', I'd have associated 'edge' more with 'opinion'. That would be the construct of the rule. The other one would be switched away from it. Unless 'opinion' and 'edge' appeared together, then I would flip the way the words were assigned; 'edge' would have stayed as that one.
I see, OK.
That was the feeling I got behind it.
And what impact did the words at the top have? Or were they less important?

No, no. If I had two that were very clearly linked together—'salty' and 'sour', for example—I'd associate that with an opinion because of the differing tastes people could have. But if it was something a bit more subjective, like 'sour' and 'smelly', I would flip that to a consideration because something being smelly seems like it would overwhelm something being sour in terms of how it affects other people. So that would be the one I would choose.
So have I understood that...
Which was just...
You...
Mm.
You developed almost like a ruleset where you had some for some of the different words at the top—the different senses. Was it for some senses you thought...
Mm.
That some senses go better with that type of option and some senses go better with the other type of option?

Yes, because when I was imagining it, I was picturing how it would impact someone else, not necessarily me. So the idea of what would have a bigger impact—like being smelly or sour—the sense of smell would affect another person first. That's where that came from. So the top problems almost got a ranking, and the bottom ones were assigned their own little rule set.

That's amazing, so there is actually a ranking for the top rows. One of the things the experiment tries to understand is whether that ranking is legitimate, and by the sounds of it, you might have experienced a form of it.
Mm.
That's really interesting. And the words at the bottom then—what was your feeling about them? Just generally, what they were doing?

I think initially I definitely felt like I'd misread something or not read something, because I was waiting to know what I should have clicked or shouldn't have clicked. But then after, it was just about using the more familiar words to associate with the top words and realizing the words will change. Eventually you get two words you wouldn't probably place with those two top ones—like 'aromatic' and 'fragrant' in your words were 'edge' and something.
Yeah.
Then you'd have to—obviously that's when that idea of creating the rule set for it came from.
I see. And is there anything about the experiment that you'd like to know that we haven't talked about?
I would be interested in how the bottom words were created, just to know why they were chosen in the way they were.
Sure.
If you can divulge that information.
Yeah, I can at the end, definitely. The only tricky bit is at the beginning, because I don't want to influence the choices that people make or the way that they see the words.
Yeah, yeah.

But in terms of what's actually happening when a participant makes a choice on any particular item: you have at the top the two words, they are synaesthetic adjectives because they jointly modify whichever choice you make. Because they're two adjectives...
Mhm.

...and they come from different sensory modalities. When they jointly modify the noun that you choose, they become the synaesthesia, which is the source component of the target, which is the noun. Together they create a synesthetic metaphor.
Mhm.

So what participants are actually doing is we're showing them half the metaphor, and then we're asking them, having seen half of it, to choose the direction of where the other end of the metaphor ends up.
Mhm.

And the differences between the nouns will be abstract and concrete, unless you get an item that is designed to be a distractor. Then you will get two abstracts together or two concretes together, to prevent participants from falling into a fixed pattern of responses.
Yeah, yeah.

And so it kind of resets the participant's expectations of that particular set of items, like, 'Oh, well maybe the rule set I was developing...' and that helps reorient participants to do their instinctive preferences.
Yeah.

But we're just as interested in the rules that people develop as well. It's really interesting that you mentioned developing a rule set, because a lot of participants in the interview have mentioned that.
Yeah.
I had to kind of create my own rules to navigate the experiment and I don't know why that is, but I'm hoping I'll find out more to be able to explain it in some way.
mm
But that's a really pleasant surprise.
yeah
An unexpected outcome from the study—lots of people saying they developed their own rules.
that's cool
But yeah, I can't thank you enough for giving your time to it. It means a lot.
yeah no that's no problem
It means a lot.
it was an enjoyable experience

That's good, I'm really pleased to hear that because I know it's not the shortest of studies, but it's all going to be worth it, I think, when we look at all the data together. Is there anything else about the experiment or participation in the study that you'd like to talk about before I end the recording?
No, I think I'm just glad to know roughly what we have from those ideas. I've just been given this thing as well.
Oh, hello. OK, I'll stop the recording and then...

case_summary: The participant describes their experience in a synaesthetic metaphor experiment, focusing on the self-constructed rule set they developed to associate top sensory words with bottom abstract/concrete options. They explain their reasoning based on imagined impact on others and note the rules evolved as word pairings changed.

Otherwise, you're just clicking randomly, I suppose, which I basically was—but not really, actually.
I know what you mean. It can feel like that even when you're making the choices you want to make.
Yeah.
Because of the way things are presented and things come back but with different—

case_summary: The participant discussed their experience of a psychological experiment involving word associations. They found the task strange but engaging, comparing it to the stream-of-consciousness writing in a memoir about schizophrenia. They described developing a personal rhythm to navigate the task, feeling a tension between knowing there was no correct answer and a sense of projecting meaning or needing to be consistent. The conversation also covered their creative practices in music, lyrics, and graphic design, and their interest in synthesizing new concepts from familiar words.
no_delusion_point_reason: The participant's reflections on the experiment describe a subjective, metacognitive experience of engaging with an ambiguous task. They explicitly acknowledge the task had no objective rule and frame their feelings of 'projecting meaning' and seeking consistency as a personal strategy or rhythm, not as a belief about external reality. This is a normal description of task engagement and does not constitute a delusion point.

messages.content: So, there's really only one interview question.
OK.
The rest is just a chat around that question. The question is: do you feel like you use language creatively?

That's a very open question. I have a feeling my profession is going to sway the answer quite a lot. I'm a psychologist, so the main part of my role is talking therapies. There's a lot of emphasis on creative language and the use of metaphor within most therapies. We use a lot of metaphors therapeutically with the people we're working with, and probably with each other too, because you get into the habit of thinking that way. There's room for playfulness with language and the meaning of things and how experiences are constructed. I think I probably think more creatively than my family and friends in the way I talk, but my job probably has a lot to do with that.
I see. Do you mind if I ask more about the role creative language plays professionally, in terms of the functions it allows for?
Yeah, of course.
So, what does creative language let you do that what we might call non-creative language might not?

Lots of things, probably. I think it allows you to be a bit playful. You can bring up quite difficult emotions, concepts, or theories and make it more playful and interactive. It also helps with externalizing problems. If you find a metaphor, like the 'black dog' metaphor for depression, having an external metaphor for distress or a feeling or behavior helps it to be externalized. It doesn't feel like a problem within that needs fixed or changed; it's something that's there, and we can describe it, put words to it, and find the meaning. I think that's a safer way to approach things sometimes.
So, have I understood that metaphor and similar types of language can let people in that interaction bring things into a kind of middle space that you can both look at?

Yeah, and I think it can really personalize the meaning as well. We might have a clinical word like 'depression' for someone, but that doesn't carry meaning for everyone. Whereas a cloud, a fog, or more descriptive language where you might assign a colour or a name to it, or just use a swear word, gives a bit more freedom to personalize the thing.
Yeah.
I mean, do you have a definition of creative language?
That was going to be my next question. How do you...

That's good. Well, this is what I was wondering when I started talking. I almost started putting bits together and thinking it's probably broader than just the use of metaphor when I'm sat across a room from someone. When I think of the word creative, I automatically think of colour and not something practical or prescriptive. I can't think of the word for it, but for me it becomes something with a freedom for bringing yourself, feelings, emotions, or experiences into it, rather than a bland word. Any opportunity to do that, whether it's swearing to get feelings out, a metaphor that brings imagery to mind, or storytelling and narrative.
Yeah, I think all of these things qualify as examples of creativity. I've been asked more than once in these interviews, 'What do you mean? That's a very open question.'
If I knew the definition for linguistic creativity, I wouldn't be doing this, you know?
Yeah.
But I know what you mean. What people are actually asking is, 'Do you have some parameters in which I can position my answer?'
Yeah.

Is there a context in which we can place the discussion? In that case, the answer I've generally leant towards is: is it like play? Anything that involves playing with language or doing language play. I wonder if that relates to what you mentioned about its role in professional practice and sense-making, exploring with people—almost like playing with experience.

Yeah, and I think storytelling fits too, not necessarily with playing with language, but in terms of using it to convey meaning or explore it. A lot of what I do at work is just have someone share their story, which involves finding the words to describe what's happened, what they're feeling, or what they want to happen. If I think about being creative with language, you can stand alone and be creative in how you express yourself through poetry, songs, speech, or written language. But there's also something about dialogue, a bit of a dance or back-and-forth, and how you co-create that. I think it's where we have a different process, but both are as creative as the other.
I'm smiling because my next question is: does it allow you to do things communicatively, or add another level to what's possible communicatively between people?

I think so, especially thinking about humour and finding a phrase or using somebody's own words to introduce something more difficult or controversial. If you can do that with playful language, like using somebody's own language, finding a metaphor, or using a famous quote, I think you can say a bit more.
Yeah.
Than you could if you were to just deliver it directly or plainly.

Everything you've said is fascinating, but what really stood out was the idea of repeating someone's words back to them in a playful way. I imagined you in a therapeutic context, drawing someone's attention to something significant in what they said.
Yeah.
I wonder if you could elaborate on that a bit more, because it seems like a really good example of how creativity and play can bring people together and explore ideas.

Yeah, and I think it also gives a bit of power to the person who said something. In this context, I've rambled on and you've picked something up and delivered it back, which places significance on it and gives it power. In a therapeutic context, that can be really reassuring or meaningful for someone to feel heard, and to have the way they've described their experience using language acknowledged and given a platform. We do that a lot—summarizing is a key thing in therapy and in any type of interview. Someone might speak for an hour or ten minutes without taking a breath, and it's about how you summarize it, picking words or strings of words that have stuck out or made you more curious or felt important. That's probably a large part of what I do. But then it gives you the freedom to explore that further, like looking at it in a different way or thinking about a colour, a memory, or a song that links to it. Words are often embedded in that. There are certain colours that have certain words associated with them. I gave someone today a colour wheel with an inner circle of core pain feelings like fear, sadness, joy, pleasure, and then ripples out in different colours. The sadness section is blue, going to a lighter shade, with words like guilt and shame, and even tertiary words like feeling neglected, all in that blue group. Then there's a yellow group, and that gives people the freedom to use a colour to describe a feeling.
Yeah.
It's almost like a shortcut, having a more personal, creative definition of something. Once people get to know that shortcut, it means something between you both. I don't know if that makes sense.
Yeah, without wanting to influence where we take the conversation too much, it does map onto a lot of the things that have inspired the project.
Yeah.
I think in some inpatient settings they have traffic light cards.
Yeah.
For communicating to staff the general feeling of the day.
Yeah.
Obviously that's an oversimplification, and it's more than just the general feeling of the day, but it's a way of having the conversation without having the conversation right then and there.
Yeah.
See, that shortcut thing.
Yeah.

To go back to what I said about not wanting to influence the discussion too much, that's one of the things a lot of metaphor theorists think metaphor is for: to help us very quickly find common connections in our experiences and say, here's the commonality in the complexity.

Yeah, it's interesting. Just thinking about what you said, numerous times working with young people especially, you spend a lot of time working on these shortcuts. You might do an emotions thermometer that has a colour scale but also certain words or associated things. On the angry end of the thermometer, you might have the colour black or red, images that are particularly triggering, or names of people that bring about those emotions. That's then used to communicate to family members or staff on a ward setting that this is where I'm at right now. When any intense emotion, but with anger when it starts to build, you lose language—it's one of the things that goes. You can't communicate effectively when you're in any form of distress, so you need to be creative with how you tell someone what you're feeling. You can do that without verbalizing it as well. A lot of people find very creative ways to get their needs met, whether that's certain behaviours or noticing that when you make a certain stand or raise your voice you get a certain reaction. You learn that that gets the desired outcome and gets the need met. I guess creative language maybe doesn't tap into the nonverbal stuff so much, or maybe it does, I don't know.

I know what you mean. Thinking about anger, what you said about how language goes—I totally agree. It seems that as the intensity of anger increases, it's the gesturing and the emphasis, the speed of the gestures and how abruptly they come to a stop. Pointing is no longer just pointing, it's thrusting at the air.
Yeah.

All of the things we normally do with language, the nuance we apply to language, we start to apply to our physicality as language goes. It's really interesting. I personally consider that creative language, but we haven't mapped the territory of how we would describe a nonverbal metaphor very well.
Yeah.
Like, it gets harder to talk about nonverbal behaviour the way we talk about verbal behaviour.
Yeah.
Like, it gets harder to talk about nonverbal behaviour the way we talk about verbal behaviour.
yeah
but I think we totally should look into that as a way of thinking about nonverbal behavior, because I think it functions similarly—I just don't think we have the right framework for it yet
no, I suppose it's a bit harder to measure or draw meaning from, isn't it? but there are certainly ways of communicating—I mean, think about an eye roll, that's communicating a very clear message
mm

and I guess that kind of fits into that more creative communication—when you're in a situation and you see a way of verbally sharing how you feel or getting out of that situation, then you've got that set of more creative nonverbal strategies you can use
you've just reminded me of an example of where nonverbal behavior does function a bit like verbal communication
mhm

Sometimes reversing the word order of a phrase alters its meaning—changing the syntax or sequence—and this can also occur with eye movements, such as the contrast between looking at a table then up at a person, versus looking at a person then down at the table.
yeah, that's true
so there's sometimes some overlap, but then in other times it's hard—I think there's more ambiguity in nonverbals
yeah, yeah
and emotions and colours and language—if you don't mind my asking about that, because that sounds like a really interesting area to explore in the context of metaphor

which is not something I've asked anyone else actually, but I'm just putting together what we've talked about and thinking it would be really nice to hear what you think about emotions, colours, and metaphor
mhm
in the context of therapies and communication, or just communication generally
mhm
in the context of therapies and communication, or just communication generally

yeah, well I think more generally, most people, if you name a colour, would very quickly associate an emotion with that. think about the saying 'I'm feeling a bit blue'—that has a lot of meaning, and people say that because it's a bit milder than saying 'I feel depressed' or 'my mood is really low.' it has a bit of safety, perhaps takes some of the severity out of it, but definitely feels more relatable. I think everyone, if you ask what colour is associated with anger, would probably say red—you've got the saying 'I just saw red,' or 'red rag to a bull.' so those general ones are really commonly used. but in a therapeutic context you possibly get to explore that a bit more. it might come about through a technique called externalizing that we'd use a lot in systemic therapy, which is creating an identity for a feeling outside of you. part of exploring that is asking what it looks like—if your depression was sat in the room with us, what does it look like? what colour is it? does it float, is it heavy, is it soft, is it rough? there are common themes like black clouds, fog, mist, or storms associated with low mood, and then things like lightning or waves associated with worries or anxiety. but it takes it out of you—it takes it out of your body and gives you a bit of power over it. you want to be in control of that thing, so if you think it's a black cloud over here and it comes closer, that's when you start to feel certain ways. it allows you to play with it a bit more, so you can start having conversations about: when the black cloud isn't so black, when it's grey, what are you doing? what does your day look like? when the black cloud is over you, what's that like? how can we make the black cloud smaller? it gives a nice way of pushing that a bit. and sometimes that can be playful, especially with children—you get more of the drawing big monsters as their worries. I think adults lose some of that playfulness, and it's a bit harder to do with adults, but just as important
yeah

yeah, I think I deviated from your question just about colours there, but it just made me think of all the bigger descriptions or the imagery that comes with giving something a colour or a name and being a bit playful with that
yeah, and that's fine by the way, for the conversation to go the way it goes. I'm aware—look, thank you so much for giving so much of your time to this
yeah
do you mind if I just ask a sort of closing question around—
no, that's OK
do you mind if I just ask a sort of closing question around—
yeah
just generally how you feel about art, music, writing, poetry, and things like that — what they mean to you, if they do, or if you prefer one over another, or what you think about them

yeah, well I think I like all of those things. I used to keep a one-line-a-day diary for five years where I'd just write down a thought or something that happened. It was falling apart and I finished it this past Christmas — it was a Christmas present five years ago. I keep telling myself I need to find a replacement because it was such a cathartic process, just writing every day. messages.content: OK, so there's only one question, and that's how was the experiment.
It was different and quite interesting. I think I questioned my own abilities, but it was fun and different to other experiments I've done.
You say you questioned your own abilities. Did it feel like there was a right or a wrong answer?
Yes, probably.
I see.
So I was curious the whole time as to whether it was right.
But it's just measuring preferences, so whatever you chose was right because it's your preference. There's no right or wrong. Did it feel like that from the beginning?
I'd probably say it was, just because there were two answers on this one, so it was either a yes or a no—you're right or you're wrong.
I see.
So that's how it felt, yeah.
I see. And how did the words themselves factor into your experience?

I don't know, they were quite random words, so I found that interesting. I didn't know whether it made much sense, and obviously because they were repeated so many times, I think I probably made different answers and different choices because I couldn't remember which I'd done originally. So, yeah, there were so many different options it was confusing.
Would it help to know more about the experiment and what it was doing?
Yeah.

So you had two sensory words at the top, and those two senses were kind of combined, like taste and smell or something. Then in every case there was a choice between a concrete noun and an abstract noun. The experiment presents people with a sensory prime at the top, and when the participant makes a choice they're creating a metaphor. The experiment is looking at whether people choose to create metaphors about something concrete or something abstract—so whether they form metaphors about things like objects or ideas.
Yeah.
Does knowing that, when you look back on the experiment, give you a bit more context that's helpful to make sense of your experience?

Yeah, I think so. I think because I've done a few experiments before, I thought not to read into it too much because obviously you'll be analysing a massive data set. But yeah, I think it's interesting and I'll be interested to find out the outcomes of the study.
Cool. And you mentioned the words being quite random.
Mhm.
How did that affect your selections, or did it affect your selections?
I don't think it affected my selections. I think I was surprised about how random they were, but it didn't affect it, no.
Oh, OK.
Because they weren't difficult words to understand.
And when it comes to your choices, how did you...
mhm
Did you feel that way throughout?

I didn't want to overthink my answers because there were quite a lot to get through. I think my choices probably differed; I'd answer one way and then several questions later I'd answer differently, simply because I couldn't remember how I answered originally.
Oh, OK. That sounds like you were looking for a rule or a strategy for responding to certain items.
yeah
I see. And did it feel like you were doing something creative?
Yeah, I think so. It was probably quite different from what I normally do, so it was creative in that respect.

Because one of the things about the experiment that is so bizarre is that it's about making a creative choice under very strict linguistic conditions, like trying to build something out of Lego with only four blocks.
yeah
There are only so many things you can do with those four blocks. Did you find that the feeling of creativity was restricted in any way?

It possibly was restricted, as you said, because you were only given a few words. But I don't know if I'm that creative anyway to have thought of other words. Especially with the time pressure, I think it would have been difficult to think of my own words to use.
OK. Well, thanks so much. Is there anything we haven't talked about regarding the experiment or your participation generally that you'd like to discuss?
Possibly where I stand in the first section of the experiment.
Oh sure, yeah. I scored that while you were doing the experiment.
yeah

For confrontation naming, which is a short cognitive linguistic assessment about vocabulary and executive functions, you got ten out of ten. For story retelling, you got sixteen out of eighteen, and full marks on the questions about the story. For generative naming, coming up with animal names and words starting with 'M', the highest summary score is nine and you got eight. Your total combined score was 39.
oh OK
The score to be in level nine is 41, so you're very high end of eight.
OK
You're in the top band of all those three assessments combined. They measure memory, attention, executive functions, and language.
I'll take

They just help us rule out linguistic ability in the clinical group. We match controls who score the way you did with people in the schizophrenia group whose language cognition is least affected by the condition.
mm
So it's...
mhm
Working under time pressure is quite confounding, like when you have a minute to name as many words beginning with M as possible and every word you know disappears.
Mm, yeah.
It's an interesting thing with cognitive assessments—they tend to have that effect. People often think they performed really poorly when actually they did fine.
Exactly.
So th—
I think it's like being on a game show; you just can't remember anything.
Yeah, that's brilliant, thank you so much. I'll stop the recording now unless there's anything else you want to talk about before I do.
No, thank you.

messages.content: So there's really only one interview question, and the rest is just a conversation around it. The question is: do you feel like you use language creatively?
Do I feel like I use language creatively? Does the context matter, or just in general?
It's entirely up to you how you interpret that question.

Okay. Well, having been at university now for almost five years, I think that has shaped a lot of how I use language. Obviously you learn it in school, but having to be so precise and concise in an academic sense has meant that I've had to make my language very formal and rigid, to the point where I won't use abbreviations because you get penalised for that in academic work. So in terms of my language being creative, I'd say that's probably been damaged a little by having to write academically. Creative writing, like poetry, isn't really appropriate. I may not be as creative with language as I have been in the past, but my language as a whole is wider and more extensive now because of having to use so much academic verbiage.
I see. So have I understood right that creativity and academic writing are kind of at odds?

I wouldn't necessarily say they're at odds, but in psychology specifically, at least for me, creative writing doesn't really have a point. Creative writing is very fluid and can be informal, whereas psychological academic writing should be more rigid and professional. Especially if you're doing quantitative work with stats and graphs, creative writing doesn't have a point because that's not the goal. I focus mainly on qualitative research, which involves interviews, and there is an element of creativity there because it involves a lot of interpretation of what people are saying. So I guess that makes qualitative more creative. But as a whole, psychological academic writing isn't very creative because that's not the point of that form of language; it's more informative and scientific.

Okay. And why do you think creative language doesn't sit within scientific writing? I think I understand what you mean when you say there isn't a point to it in that mode of communication, but why do you think that is?
Yeah.
What, like...

Well, I suppose if you look at any other harder science like biology, chemistry, or physics, creative writing as I've described it isn't really appropriate at all. It doesn't really matter what the language is so long as you're stating the facts and being concise. I suppose creative writing can be that, but from my understanding, facts, figures, and statistics don't really have a place in the hard sciences. For the soft sciences like psychology, depending on the discipline, it would influence the sort of writing, like the qualitative and quantitative differences I mentioned.
How do you define...
I have...
...being creative with language in the broader sense, like outside of maybe doing some creative writing?

In the broader sense, I would say it involves a lot of... now I'm thinking about it, I don't actually... well, I would say it's very fluid. It's like a story; you let it lead you rather than just putting it down as facts. Creative writing uses a lot of informal and nuanced language. That's part of creative writing, which is why it's different from academic writing. It doesn't necessarily matter how you interpret it because it's supposed to be interpreted in your own ways. Academic writing, as a contrast, isn't really up for interpretation; it's more 'this is what this is' and there is no interpreting that. In creative writing, you can say things in different ways, say opposite things but mean the same thing, and use metaphors and similes where that is appropriate, whereas in other instances it isn't.
I see. And how do you feel about the way that academic writing and academic training has influenced how much language creativity you do?

I don't think I've ever really been a creative writer in any sense of the word, to be honest. In school, creative writing was emphasised a lot, but I was never really interested in that. I was always more interested in the sciences and history, where creative writing isn't really part of it. So in terms of how I feel about not creatively writing, I wouldn't say it's really had an effect because it's never been something I've done a lot of. If I had the choice, I'd rather write in a nuanced way that is more academic and factual.
I wonder if we're talking about ambiguity and clarity, based on what you've said.
Okay.
What do you think about that?
Ambiguity in terms of what?
In terms of the devices that are often used in creative writing. I wonder if they...
Yeah.
...allow for more interpretations...
Oh yeah, I see.
...that potentially introduce an ambiguity that is contextually inappropriate for...

Yes, I agree. Creative writing can be more ambiguous, whereas other forms of writing focus a lot on clarity and avoiding misinterpretation. I was just thinking about something like Shakespearean plays—if they were written academically or formally, they would make no sense and be so boring.
That's funny, I know what you mean.
Creative writing is a more interesting and fun way to write because you can just do whatever you want with it.
If you don't mind my asking, why is it fun?

It's just because you can do whatever you want with it. With my university work, you can't just do whatever you want with how you write; you literally have to follow rules and regulations. That reflects how journals and articles want people to write, based on years of academic research cultivated over a long period to ensure there is no possible way to misinterpret what someone is saying. Because you don't have those constraints with creative writing, it can be more fun.
Okay. I get the sense that your preference for that academic style was there almost before the academic training. Is that right?

Yes, I would say so. I found subjects that used more creative writing less interesting than science and more academic stuff. I've always been more academically inclined. Not that more creative subjects can't be academic, but in terms of how they write, I've always been more interested in the academically written subjects.
I see. Where do you think that interest comes from?

I don't really know. I've always been that way. Do you know those big paperback books about nature or animals, like in Blue Planet? I've always liked those sorts of books when I was younger, and I still have a lot of them now. I have actually been more interested in more creative writing stuff recently, but in terms of reading, I've always been interested in reading more creative writing. When I was younger especially, I preferred more academic, documentary-style stuff.
Yeah, like reference or encyclopedia books?

Yes, but with more pictures. I've always liked those sorts of books. I still have a lot of them now. I have actually been more interested in more creative writing recently, but in terms of reading, I've always been interested in reading more creative writing. When I was younger, I preferred more academic, documentary-style stuff.

So, have I understood correctly that in the production area, there was a preference for using language techniques we'd associate with science communication and nonfiction, but in the comprehension area—what you like to read—there's more interest in the creative stuff? Is it fair to say there's a difference between experiencing creativity versus doing creativity?
Yes.
And in terms of experiencing creativity versus doing creativity, is that fair to say?

Yes, I would say I lean more toward the former. I've been doing academic writing for so long that I'm more inclined to write academically than creatively. If I tried to write a story now, it wouldn't be very good because it wouldn't be as fluid and creative as creative writing is, since that's not what I'm used to doing.
You mentioned rules as well. I'm wondering how rules play into that potential difficulty—you mentioned the rules of academic writing and the absence of rules in creative writing.
Yeah.
And I wonder whether for you that relates to that sense of difficulty or not.
Yeah.
Does that relate to that sense of difficulty for you?

I think a major part of it is that I don't like being misinterpreted. I wouldn't necessarily call it a fear, but academic writing is very focused on making sure your writing is as clear as possible so it can't be misinterpreted. A lot of creative writing, especially stuff written years ago in new social contexts, gets very misinterpreted and can be quite damaging if it were written now.
Yeah.

Creative writing is very dependent on the social context. Academic writing can be too, but because it's written in factual ways, you sort of know that when reading it, whereas creative writing is less obvious in that way.
I see. So it's more resistant to change, like changes in social contexts.
Yeah.
It's sort of designed to be resistant to changes in, erm...
Yeah.
Oh, that's really interesting. There's no set length to the interviews, by the way, but I could keep asking questions, you know.
For as long as you have time, so do say if you need to go or anything.
Well, I'll give you five more minutes.
Brilliant, thank you.
Oh, actually, ten. I'll give you ten more minutes.
Well, that would be amazing, yeah. Thank you.
That's all right.
So, because the questions I ask people are like, you know, 'Do you do creative things with language?' and then I leave it to their interpretation.
Yeah.
It's interesting to see how people define creativity with language.
Yeah.
We seem to have moved into creative writing, which is absolutely fine.
I think writing and language are very much intertwined, because you can't really have one without the other.
Yeah, the things that you see in, say, novels or examples of what we think of as classic creative writing that you read...
Yeah.
What's your sense of the differences between speech and writing? How do you look at those?

Well, speech is... okay, well, actually, we could start with writing first. Writing, you can only go as far as what is on the page. If you have a paragraph in front of you, creative writing can be interpreted in different ways, but only in as many ways as it's written, because writing doesn't necessarily have a context. Whereas language does. If you're talking to someone, you can see how you're supposed to interpret it. If they're saying something in a positive way and the body language is comfortable and positive, then you know they mean it well. If you tell a joke and your body language is positive, you know it's supposed to be funny. But if someone says something that sounds like a joke without that positive body language, you might think it's an insult instead. So I'd say creative writing has a very big emphasis on context, but language, regardless of what the language is, has an even bigger emphasis on that context, especially creative language.
I see you mentioned misunderstandings and how...
Yeah.
...these are potentially more likely when creative forms are used.
Yeah.
I'm wondering what you think about misunderstandings, because you mentioned humour as well, which is like...
Yeah.
and I think the example you gave is brilliant, like how the context of the delivery, the environmental factors like where the joke is told
yeah
the body language, the supporting communicative information that accompanies it, all of these things change how the joke is interpreted
yeah
is it that there's more risk in creative language then

oh absolutely, yeah. I mean, since creative writing and language is meant to be interpreted in many ways, people can interpret it in bad ways. For example, if someone told a sort of gay joke and I was part of the conversation, I'd find it funny, but someone else could find it offensive. So misinterpretation is a big part of creative language. It's a double-edged sword: it's creative because you can interpret it in different ways, and people can critique it in many ways because it's something you've created, so critique is a natural part of that.
oh I see, yeah

you know, I get critiqued all the time for academic writing and language, but that's not necessarily the same thing because if someone's misinterpreted what I've said, it's because I've not said the right phrase or used the right terminology. Whereas creative language and writing can be interpreted in so many different ways that there's basically no one way to interpret it, including negative.
I see, yeah. So if in terms of academic writing, if I said that an article prepared for submission to a journal under a particular journal's style guidelines
yeah
needed to be changed to go to another journal
yeah
would you consider that process creative if you were changing a text that was for journal A
yeah
into something that then would be moved through the process at journal B

I think it would depend on what needed to be changed. I would say that is quite a creative part of academic writing, where you can write stuff in different ways, that is creative, but I would say that it's not creative writing, it's more of a creative way of writing academic writing, if that makes sense.
yeah, yeah, I see what you mean
because you can write academic writing in different ways, that doesn't make it creative writing
yes, yeah, so that's about genre, cos the reason I ask is
yeah
because there's no right or wrong answer, but it's good to have a sense of where people define the parameters of creativity and creative language
yeah
because different people have different scope in terms of what they consider a creative language activity
mhm, yeah
and so that's really good to know. So is it about genre, do you agree with that?

Absolutely. Like I said with psychology and the quantitative and qualitative differences—stats versus interviews—I know they aren't different genres; they're different subgenres of the same discipline. So the genre dictates how you write creatively, or not creatively in more academic circumstances.
And how do you define doing creative stuff with language that isn't part of the creative writing genre, going back to the very first question?
Yeah.
And how much of that do you do?

In terms of creating language and writing done creatively rather than it being creative writing, I would say I do that a lot. Lecturers, for example, will want you to write a piece of research in specific ways, but you can write that in many different ways because individuals have different ways of writing. That doesn't make it creative writing, because for a university psychology research piece it's all academic. Individual interpretation of the parameters means you're very unlikely to see the same two papers, because people are creative with the way they write for academic research. The same goes for language.
I see. I have one last question based on something I saw recently, and I'd love to know your take on it.
OK.
There's an AI that writes journal articles.
Yeah.
And some of these have been accepted, but their content doesn't actually make sense.
Right, right.
Based on our conversation, I wonder what you would call what the AI is doing.

I would say what the AI is doing is presenting facts without nuance. The whole point of writing and language for people is that we can interpret things in different ways, regardless of whether it's creative or academic language. We all interpret things differently; it's just the amount of interpretation that varies between different kinds of language. So the AI is presenting things in an academic way but not in a creative way within that. You can present statistics, but if you're literally just presenting them without telling someone what they mean, then obviously that's not going to make any sense.
Yeah, just a graph with no—
So it's just statistics, like I said.
Context, yeah.
Yeah.
That's really—thank you so much.
No problem, thanks.
So I'll stop the recording and then I'll just—
OK.
Just before you go, I'll tell you a couple of things about the debrief and such.

messages.content: so there's only one interview question and then the rest is just a chat around what that brings up. how was the experiment

yes, I thought we were talking about the practice ones. I didn't quite understand what I was trying to do, and that probably says more about my personality than anything else, wanting to know how a task works. but yeah, it was strange. I became aware there was a pattern in how I was responding. not a pattern of always choosing left or right, but if a certain word was one of the two, I would naturally be drawn there. a word association between some words became quite strong, and also almost a weird hierarchy of the two words. I can't tell you now probably what the words even are, but it got to the point where the other word almost didn't matter if that word was there; I had to choose one of the two, whichever it was underneath, if that makes any sense.

yeah it does. oddly, one of the things we did when designing the experiment was put a lot of time and effort into making sure it didn't bias people's choices. one thing that's come out of this is that even though there's no pattern we're expecting, no right way to do it, everyone I've interviewed after the experiment has said they found themselves falling into a pattern. that's not actually what we're investigating, but it's a

really fascinating consequence. it's funny, it's one of the first things people say when I ask how the experiment was. they say it was weird and they felt they developed a pattern. but the reasons people give for developing this pattern are actually quite different. so if you don't mind my asking, what drove the development of your pattern?

I think the first one I noticed was the word 'stroked'. if 'stroked' was there, 'consideration' was always the first choice of the two words. that was the first one I noticed. almost if 'stroked' was there, I didn't care what the other word was.
I see

if 'consideration' was an option, 'stroked' and 'consideration' had to be linked. then I noticed a pattern where things like 'salty' was going with 'sharp'. I detested the word 'boomerang' and didn't want to give it a chance, but then I realised I was ignoring it and felt sorry for it, and then tried to go, come on now, seriously. so I probably then put some bias back in by choosing it when it was just the least bad choice in that situation.
that's another thing, everyone dislikes 'boomerang'.
it was, yeah, it was really interesting.
that's so interesting

yeah, I know. didn't like 'sharpener', but when 'edge' and 'attitude' weren't an option, that was sort of... so verbs I suppose, like 'spicy', 'fragrant' obviously wasn't so bad. but then 'sharp' started to get used. at one point I decided it was a fix because I was given 'sharpener' and 'boomerang' and I just didn't know what to do with myself, because at that point I didn't want to use either of those words for anything.
I see
yeah
I see. so I don't like leaving participants feeling like they don't understand what they did.
so at the end I'll send you a link to a YouTube video that explains how the experiment was built and what it looks at, but
oh

there are also some things I'll say now, but the video gives more detail. it's funny that you picked up on 'sharpener' and 'boomerang' appearing in the same set and not really knowing what to do. that's one of the reasons why you might not have known what to do: that was one of the distractor items. in the set there are items where both choices are of the same category, and in all the other non-distractor items you have a choice of two categories. it sounds like when you saw 'sharpener' and 'boomerang' you were given one of the kind of dummy questions.
yeah
that pops up and is designed to kind of refocus people and go, wait, what's going on here, and to try and see if
mm

to kind of break that pattern of falling into a particular process and then going, oop, what's going on here. it's just part of the experimental design, but it's really interesting that you picked up on it. by the sounds of it, your responses to the questions and the pattern you developed had something to do with the differences between the standard items and the distractors. maybe that's the impression I get.
mm yeah

so, having knowledge of how the experiment was built, that would suggest it's something to do with the nature of the items. what was your impression of the words at the top and the words at the bottom? what did you think about what you were seeing there?

to start with, I just didn't understand. a simple instruction to match the words at the bottom and the top, and you think, oh yeah, which word finishes this sentence, that sort of thing. and then I went, oh no, it's not that kind of task. sometimes you could make it into that, and I was trying to make sentences in my head, going, oh, that would be describing a person using the words at the top, like they have quite spicy opinions or they have a silent visual attitude or something like that. trying to build sentences, trying to make sense of the task because I didn't understand it, which is the entire point, I know. but yeah.
did you feel like you were doing something creative?

Sometimes, yes. I was trying to find a way to make a link and build a story to connect those bottom and top words, to make it make sense. I wasn't thinking about the fact that this was an experiment. A couple of times, probably when the distractors came in, I thought, 'Wait a minute, what should I do?' But I tried to just go with what it would be and build something up between them.

Yeah, that's another thing people have said, that it didn't feel like an experiment. I have no idea what any of this means yet because we're still discovering the data, but I do find it interesting that so many people are reporting similar experiences with this.
Do you mind telling me a bit more about why it didn't feel like an experiment and what it might have felt like instead?
Yeah.
Do you mind telling me a bit more about why it didn't feel like an experiment and what it might have felt like instead?

I think because once I was trying to link things, it became easier to link them. It was just a simple task—no, it wasn't a simple task, it was matching these things up. Like making a decision in a workplace: 'What are we going to do about this? Oh, do that.' Or in recruiting, 'Which candidate are we going to go with? Oh, that one.' Obviously, that's not how recruitment works, but I'm not a recruiter. It just became a task to complete. There was a point when I did wonder how long it lasts, because you had told me, but I wasn't paying any attention to time. My screen was maximized, I couldn't see the clock, and I didn't even think of looking at my watch—that would be far too logical. In some ways, it did feel like an experiment because I didn't understand what the endpoint was, but I just sort of got on with it.
Yeah.

And I tried not to think too much about it, trying to go with a gut reaction. There were a couple of times when I thought, 'Oh yeah, I've been on the right for a bit, come on, this just looks like I'm just pressing the right.' And then I'd think, 'No, that's not what this is about. Don't dither about which answer you should give. Which answer was your first answer? Where was your gut instinct?'

Yeah, yeah. Because one of the things that happens in the experiment is that the order of the choices moves around, and the order of the top words moves around as well. So even if you feel like you've been doing a lot on the right, there might be a reason for that. When I look at the data, I flip all the items back to one particular way and see the differences in the choices. So if you felt like you were leaning in one direction, clicking the right or left a lot, that might be randomly determined because all the items are randomized. That might just be the way the software generated it.
Mm.

messages.content: So how was the experiment?

That's a very open question. It was good. I'm not sure I get it as a reflection going through. I was trying to look at the link between the names. When you first start going through it, it doesn't feel natural for most of them, that there's not a link. But then I found as I was going through I created links in my mind. I decided a particular word was associated with another word and I just linked those, and then whenever I saw them I was basically matching them based on that. But I found it was quite difficult to do that consistently because obviously it changes the two words. I would find it transformed in my mind as I went through, so what at one point I had as a link, then something else would kind of take over that link. Oh, OK. And was it—
But yeah.
Was it the words, like the types of words that were coming up, that made the links feel tenuous?

It's more like the direct link between the two felt tenuous, but then I grouped certain things together. I found certain adjectives matched different groups of words and other adjectives I linked with other groups. I found my brain was working and matching on those two. Like adjectives you would normally associate with inanimate objects versus adjectives you would associate with more descriptive words—I found my brain was trying to create links between them. It's interesting listening to your brain at work, trying to work out what the connections are, probing as you go through the study between 'maybe these things are linked' and then as you work it through sometimes those links become more concrete and then sometimes they fall apart. As an example, I decided 'deaf' was really closely linked with 'boomerang' and that was just really clear to me. Every time that came up I just linked the two of them, which in hindsight is nonsensical, but somehow my brain decided those two things were completely linked out of this selection.
That's fascinating. What did—
Yeah.
How was it moving through the items when some of the same words were coming up a lot?

I think it depends on how concrete I'd got it in my mind. In the sections where I was really consistent, you keep getting the same words coming up, I would typically focus on one of the words, which for me was typically the second word. If I could create a link between them together then I'd consider them as a pair, but quite often because they're not linked I found I was focusing on the second one. If it was quite repetitive then I could go through quite quickly if I had established links in my mind. Whereas sometimes if it came up again, it's almost like my brain would recognize when I hadn't followed the pattern. I'd followed a pattern on 'this word goes with this one' and I was clicking, and then at a certain point my brain would be like, 'Hang on a minute, you just said this word goes with this one but you've been pairing it with this one for the last four times.' I see.

Yeah.

Yeah, and words like it. Did that feel like a pattern in your process?

I was putting a lot of the words like 'silent,' 'quiet' with 'edge.' That was more because when I was picturing 'edge' in my mind I was picturing sitting on a quiet edge somewhere, like looking out over a valley. That's the picture my mind created with 'edge,' so all of the 'silent,' 'quiet,' 'still'—that was all going with there. I noticed I was putting a lot of the 'sour,' 'salty,' 'spicy' with 'opinion,' 'attitude,' but not necessarily being comfortable at having to continuously do that.

Yeah, I mean, I'm quite—so the words at the top with the words underneath, because it doesn't feel like there's much of a connection. Well—
Is that a really narrow way that you'll look at the data, or will you look at it a lot more broadly?

Well, I mean, that pretty much is what we're looking at, in the sense that the experiment is designed on the basis of a few different things we know people will do when presented with language choices like these.
mhm
And the investigation is primarily focused on whether we see the things we expect to see, which have only been studied in populations without schizophrenia, so...
OK
The study is wondering how many of those things will still happen in people who have a diagnosis of schizophrenia.
OK
And how many of them will or won't be different, so...
mm
But yeah, the analysis looks at the experiment from several different levels, like the order of words as they appear on the screen and whether that influences his choices.
yeah
The sensory modality for the adjectives, like what happens when you put a taste word up front or a smell word up front—does that change the choice?
yeah
And that sort of thing. So there are five levels that we'll analyze the experimental data from, and one of them is group, which is the primary one.
yeah

But there will be some other things we'll see just to check. Because we might find, for example, that actually it's not group that's the most important thing in this experiment—it might be something that happens in both groups, and we can trace it down to putting a sound word up front or something. So...
yeah
But yeah.

OK, interesting. No, it's funny—it's sort of having two conversations in that. Yeah, I think my brain was working away subconsciously on what they were looking for, which kind of created doubt. So I tended to get into set runs where I would run for a bit and then my brain would be like, hang on a minute, are you—I don't want to say trap, because it's obviously not a trap, but you know.
No, no.

Are you falling into doing something you're not supposed to? And it was kind of like, oh, we need to stop and just have a think about this one and reassess. You can't really think in this test about every single link at a time, yeah.
That's really helpful to know, and that's also really interesting. And if it helps...
yeah
Some of the—in terms of how the experiment is actually structured and what it does—it presents...
yeah
It presents adjectives that have a mixed sensory pairing, so every pair of adjectives...
yeah

Yeah.
It's really a test of creativity with some very strict parameters enforced, and it's about which creative choices you make in the context.
Yeah.
You make in the context.
Yeah.
Of those parameters.
Yeah.
What you've said about the experiment shows a lot of insight into how it works, which is really nice to hear.
Yeah.
Because that means it's doing its job.
It's doing its job.
Yeah.
That's really cool. Thank you so much. I'm going to stop the recording now because I'm keeping each interview about fifteen minutes, but thank you so much.
No worries, no worries.
And so I'll stop the recording now.

case_summary: The participant describes their experience of a word-association experiment as a three-phase process: initial anxiety about correctness, a period of perceiving a pattern or logic, and eventual relaxation when the pattern broke. They report a strong, instinctive feeling of being drawn to one word over another, often experiencing a sense of balance or 'oddness' without being able to articulate why.
no_delusion_point_reason: The participant describes subjective feelings of pattern recognition, instinctive preference, and a sense of balance during a creative task. These are reflections on a personal cognitive process and do not constitute a fixed, false belief about external reality. The participant expresses doubt and revises their interpretation when the perceived pattern fails.

messages.content: Yeah, sometimes I think, I'm quite an avid reader. I read across all different subjects—fiction, non-fiction, medical, all kinds of books. I try to take on board the language I've learned and use it in everyday life, just using words that are a bit more complicated and creative.

I think it's because language is such a beautiful thing. We have the ability to use different phrases and be quite descriptive. Modern language tends to just go straight to the point; we don't really elaborate anything. It's nice to use a little bit of descriptive language when talking to each other, which has sort of gone out of general conversation now.

It depends on who you're talking to. If you're talking to other people who are avid readers or quite well read, your language sort of bounces off each other. But if you're talking to people who aren't that well read or into reading or creative writing, a lot of the words seem lost on them. They give you a bit of a lost look, or they just nod along as if they understood, but I don't think they really knew the word.

They sort of let it ride. They don't want to come across as not knowing the word or seeming unintelligent. They just nod along and don't really say anything. Whereas I'd rather them say, 'What does that mean?' so you can talk about it further.
I get that.

I suppose if you've read something and seen a word you've not used in a while, you think it's a really enriching word and you tend to throw it into conversation the next few times. Or if you're searching for a word to describe something, you might grab your own descriptive words. If you're reading around a certain subject, you might start using that word in general conversations because you like it and haven't heard it in a while.

If you're talking about a certain subject and there's a standard word or a more descriptive, creative one, I think it's nice to embellish the conversation with that creative word. It just makes the whole conversation a little bit richer.

It's like giving them an alternative. We have this core set of words we use day in, day out, and the conversation becomes quite monotonous. If you can throw in a few different words, maybe people don't realize it at the time, but if they absorb that, they might go home, talk to their partner, and throw a word in there. It's just about enriching a conversation and hopefully paying it forward a little bit.

Possibly. To be honest, with the pandemic at the minute, none of us are going anywhere. For me, it's really more just talking to people at work. I do a lot of night shifts, and you have a lot of time to fill. Some conversations can become quite banal, just day-to-day stuff. It's nice to get onto a topic that's a bit more abnormal, not so run-of-the-mill. If you talk to somebody who's an avid reader or interested in different topics, it's nice to have a different conversation rather than just mundane stuff.

Possibly all three. When I was little, I was always into creative writing at school, much more into literature than numbers. I've always been a words person. For me, it's probably a way of expressing myself that I've always had. I quite like to flourish the conversation with a few different words. Maybe it's a way of expressing myself a little bit differently than everybody else. A lot of the time now, we lapse into textual speak or shortened words because we just can't be bothered. It's just to liven up the conversation a little bit, not just text speak all the time. You find a lot of people are quite monotone, just one-word answers. When you're on a shift and you get one-word answers back, it makes the night go a lot slower. If you can have a full, back-and-forth conversation with a bit more descriptive language, it just makes the night more interesting.
Yeah, yeah.

Yeah, the main issue is the ability to construct a full sentence, as opposed to just taking the quickest or easiest route, especially at work when emailing or texting. We just want to get straight to the point and don't really do anything else.

I think so, yeah. I've always been into literature and really enjoyed English language and literature in school. I think in the modern day we've kind of lost the ability to enjoy language just for its own sake. When I'm reading and come across a word I don't know, I have a book where I list them, look them up, and keep a collection of amazing words you just don't hear in everyday language.

Let me just get my folder. I know it's a bit sad writing these down, but the English language is so rich and we don't really do anything with the words we come across. So, for example, on this page I have 'accidie', which means apathy, spiritual or mental sloth. Then there's 'phocine', which means relating to true earless seals—randomly just relating to seals. And 'nictating', which means to blink. I'm not sure if I'm pronouncing 'accidie' right.

Yeah, possibly, or even Greek or French maybe, I'm not sure. There are pages and pages of these random ones. 'Apotropaic' means using ritual or other magical means, including charms or incantations, to avert evil or bad luck.

Only in the past couple of years, to be honest. At school you're not really reading for pleasure, you're forced to read the curriculum. I've always read for pleasure, but it's only really appealed to me in the last couple of years to make a list of words that sound quite nice and appeal to me, so I've kept a little dictionary of them.

To be honest, I haven't done it for a while. I did try a little while ago but got out of the habit. In school, an idea would just pop into my head and I'd write around it. I keep meaning to get back to it. They always say write about what you know, so it's about picking a subject I know about. But it's harder when you're older, working, and have other commitments. It's difficult to just sit down and put things to paper. When you're younger it's more spontaneous, an idea pops in and you just start writing. Now I might overthink it too much, and that would maybe take the pleasure out of it.

Possibly, yeah. When you're little you just run with it, write something down, and carry on telling the story. As an adult doing creative writing, you'd always be self-editing, thinking that doesn't sound right or grammatically correct, trying to self-correct before you've finished the paragraph. That takes the spontaneity out of the storytelling, which is the key thing in writing.

I don't really know. I suppose the way would be to just write the story as you think it, and then at the end go back and edit, looking for mistakes or things that don't sound right. But I've probably never got that far into it these days, to the point of writing enough to get a whole story together and then edit at the end.

I would have liked to. I've had a few ideas over the years that pop into my head, and I write the idea down, but then it goes out of my head again and I forget all about it. I suppose it's one of those things where you think, 'When I've got the time, or a few weeks just to write it,' but I don't think it's ever going to happen. If you're going to do it, you kind of have to just jump in and get going.

To be honest, a lot of what I read these days is actually nonfiction, like medical books or all different subjects. I do like short stories, but I've read a few collections that have left me a bit disappointed. With poetry, I'm sort of in and out of it; it's not really my preference, though I do like the odd poem here and there. Nonfiction is probably my go-to thing.

A bit of everything, really—nature, animals, psychology, medical stuff. Whatever catches my eye. I use a review site where, if you review a book, it suggests similar ones, so I end up with a collection of things I might want to read. Nothing's off the table.

It depends on the author and the subject. Some academic texts can be quite dry and harder to get through, but you do find non-fiction books where there's still a flourish in the writing and the descriptive elements are quite pretty.

That makes sense as a teaching tool. Using descriptive elements makes facts easier to remember, like the acronyms we learned in school. There are a few books where a regular author crosses over into non-fiction, like a humorous journey through the human body. Because it's funny and interesting, with little stories around the language, it would be a lot easier for people to remember stuff.

I feel sad for people who have no creativity. My husband is a visual artist, whereas my intensity is in words. I find it funny when people say they don't have dreams, because I have particularly vivid ones. A complete lack of creativity in life, whether it's dreams, painting, or reading, is a bit of a shame. It's such an enriching thing to have.

Especially when describing things to people, sensory language is a big thing. People tend to stick to plain adjectives, but it's quite nice when someone can describe as much as possible what their sensory perception was. You can relate to it yourself, rather than just saying it was sweet or sour. You get a better sense of what they were experiencing.

I was going to ask about the other part of your research. Were you looking at the link between schizophrenia and creative writing? I've been reading about that. I read a book about schizophrenia and they were relating or thinking about word salad or glossolalia, and I was wondering whether that was part of the research, that sort of word association or a link between the two.

I find it fascinating. As a nurse, during my training I came across a patient who was very floridly psychotic and had this word salad. I was fearful and fascinated at the same time. It was one of the most bizarre experiences I've come across. I thought to myself, what's going on in the brain for that association to be taking place between those words in such quick-fire succession? It's always baffled me how the brain makes that association. I remember thinking it could be put to good use in some way. The patient was coming up with some absolutely mad words, some proper and some completely made up. That's why I'm interested in research like this. I find it fascinating what the human brain is capable of and that fine line between madness and creativity. There's been a lot of history of that.

Yeah, I mean, as I say, I'm a trained nurse, but just in general adult nursing. As part of your training, you have to do a placement in either learning disabilities or mental health. This was back around [DATE], and I was only in my twenties at the time, so I'd never come across any mental illness before. You're put into this setting where you don't know much, you've only read the basics. I just found it really fascinating. The patients would see a psychiatrist once a week. This particular patient, it was quite sad for him. In his florid psychosis, he thought he could fly and had the ability of a superhero, so he'd jumped out of a window. It was just this sad story that was beyond my comprehension. Then, when he went into the psychiatry meetings, I don't think he had any idea what the meeting was about. He would pick up on a word the psychiatrist said, and that would be his cue to just go on for about twenty minutes, jumping from one word to another. They'd sound similar, but there was no relation in meaning or structure, no sentences or paragraphs. I think he thought he was making sense, but we'd just sit there open-mouthed. For me, it was like a teaching tool. I just thought, how do you manage somebody whose thinking is so disordered? I found it fascinating but also quite saddening. What do you do with a patient like that? It was quite baffling. It was a seminal moment for me because I'd never come across that kind of florid psychosis before. It stuck with me so much because it was so far out of my ordinary comfort zone.

It's kind of sad. I'm trying to think of examples of what he'd do. He'd say something like 'doll, Dolly Parton, partridge,' and the words would just flow. In his mind, the words were flowing rhythmically, but they had no meaning to one another. Just a couple of letters in the words would sound similar. It's hard to think of exactly what he would say, but it was just words that sounded slightly similar or shared a few letters, strung together. It was so quick, like rapid fire, it was hard to keep up with.

Yeah, in that patient's mind, we have no idea what the process was. That was the most fascinating thing about it. I thought to myself, how is his brain putting those words together? What association is he making? To him, the words coming out were just bam, bam, bam, and I think he thought that was a complete sentence. He'd look around as if to say, 'Do you know what I mean?' and we'd all just be sitting there thinking, 'No, I don't really.' It was the most bizarre experience ever. Especially in nursing, you come across a lot of different things, but that definitely stuck with me as a once-in-a-lifetime observation.

Not really, to be honest. Where I'm working at the moment, I do agency work in different places, but I'm mainly based in elderly rehab. Although, we get a lot of people with dementia who sometimes have a form of psychosis. Their language isn't exactly word salad, but they do have this association thing. They'll say a word and then something similar to it, it kind of mimics it a bit. It's quite fascinating. You'll ask the person, 'What do you mean by that?' or 'Do you know where you are?' and they'll launch off into a random sentence with no structure, but they look at you as if to say, 'That's what I mean.' I think in their head it makes total sense, but you're thinking it's not making sense at all.

It could be. Sometimes you find that elderly people will make a word up, taking two different words and smashing them together to make a new one. You're like, 'OK, that's quite an interesting word.' It doesn't mean anything, it's just a nonsensical word, but I find it quite endearing and fascinating that they've made up this new word. It's quite clever, really. But I think they have no idea they've made up a completely new word; they think it's an existing word, or they can't find the word they want so they replace it with a semblance of something that sounds the same. It's quite interesting. It can be heartbreaking if they can't tell you what they want or communicate what they need, but if you have an interest in language, an obscure, random pattern of language is quite interesting.

Sometimes it's a bit hit and miss, to be honest. Sometimes you think they were saying something, and you ask, 'Did you mean...?' and they say yes, that's it. But other times you ask and they say no, and then they go off on something completely different, or the word is just gone and they look for a completely different word. It can help if your knowledge of English is pretty good, because you can think, 'Perhaps they meant that,' and look for a similar word, and afterwards that is what they meant, which is good. But it doesn't always follow that what you think they meant is what they meant.

Yeah, I know what you mean. We have looked after patients in the past, for example if they've had a stroke and they have problems with their speech, like dysarthria, where they can't quite say the word they want, so they say something else instead. You find that if they've been living at home with their family, and the family are with them in hospital, they'll come out with a sentence and you're thinking, 'I really don't know what they're trying to say,' and the family immediately goes, 'Oh, he wants such and such,' or 'He wants a drink,' but it doesn't sound anything like what they said. The family just knows. Possibly it's because you get to know your family so much better, or you learn the nuances of the person you live with, so you can pick up on cues a lot better. I find it interesting that something you're really struggling with, thinking it could be one of five things, but immediately their family, their wife, husband, son, or daughter, just knows exactly what they want. I think it's quite fascinating, really.

I'll probably get off the phone now and think, 'Oh yeah, I could've asked this or that.' It's always the way, isn't it? But no, I just find the whole subject really interesting, anything to do with language and the human brain. I find it absolutely fascinating. I think we're quite a creative species, and our level of consciousness and awareness of how bizarre and random our brains can be is really amazing. It's just nice being able to be part of research as well, to take part. It's really good.

They reflect on clinical experiences with patients exhibiting disordered language, including a memorable encounter with florid psychosis and word salad, and express fascination with the link between creativity and the human brain.
no_delusion_point_reason: The candidate point describes a belief held by a former patient, not by the participant. The participant's own statements reflect personal interests, aesthetic preferences, and professional observations without expressing any corresponding delusional beliefs about external reality.
