messages.content: I've just started the recording. There's really only one formal question for the interview, which is: how was the experiment?

It was quite interesting. The last part was really interesting because I wonder if there was some association with how we can have different meanings for a word—either conceptual and abstract or more descriptive. Even though for some words I didn't really know where they fit, I could somehow relate them to an attitude or opinion more than a word you'd use to describe something concrete. I was leaning more towards using them to describe something quite abstract. It was interesting, and in terms of creative writing I could see how that would create a lot of diversity in how words can be used, adding richness to a text that might not make logical sense but somehow fits.

Wow, you've tapped into a lot of what's going on in the experiment, which is great to hear. Would it help to have a brief description of what the experiment's mechanism is and what it's really measuring?
Yeah, I'd be really interested.

So the words at the top are two paired adjectives, and because they come from different senses they create a sort of synaesthetic effect, muddling up the senses. Like you pointed out, your choices are between concrete and abstract things. The experiment is really interested in whether muddling specific senses directs whether you prefer to bind them with concrete or abstract things. In your very first response to the experiment you basically described exactly what it's doing, which is really interesting. When you were moving through it, did you feel like you were doing something creative?

Yeah, I think in the back of my head I might have associated 'smelly' with a consideration. I was trying to go through it without dwelling too much, but I was thinking, in what sort of context would someone be inconsiderate but in a smelly and rough way?
Yeah.
In a smelly and rough way, like—
Yeah.

But as an attitude as well, you can sort of visualize it. When you say someone's smelly or rough, they're just not easy to get along with and there's a lot of friction in the dynamics or something like that.
Yeah.

It was also interesting—I don't know if it's true—but I thought some of the pairings came up again. I don't know if they were exactly the same, but similar ones came up. At first it was very confusing because the adjectives don't really fit either the concrete or the abstract thing exactly, so initially it was like some kind of blind association. But the more I did it, the more I thought, yeah, maybe someone could be smelly and rough in their attitude. I think I got more into it as I went along.
Oh, I see. So almost like the process of going through it made the choices more comfortable?

Yeah, I think so. I was very concrete in the way I was looking at the words at first, but the more they came up, the further along I got, I just found myself going with what seemed to flow. Towards the end I started making those associations of someone being smelly and rough, or aromatic in their attitude—that kind of thing came along further down the line.
Wow, and—
Yeah.

Of the four things on the screen at any one time—the two items at the top and the choices below—did you feel like any of them were influencing your decisions more than the others, or was it all the same?
How do you mean? Like, if that word came up then I'd more associate it with—
Did you f—
—if that word came up then I'd more associate it with…
Like, with each individual item, did you feel all four things on the screen had an equal effect on your decision, or more so the things at the top, or more so the things at the bottom?

I guess the things at the top, just because they were adjectives. Eventually the opinion, the attitude, and the consideration sort of merged into just the abstract part of it. Unless there was an adjective I could really associate with the edge or the boomerang—which there wasn't much—I did veer towards the abstract forms. I don't know if that makes any sense.
Yeah, yeah. And—
Yeah.
Why do you think that was, for you?

I think maybe towards the end I was trying to focus more on the feeling the adjectives gave to either the abstract or concrete thing. It didn't matter whether it was an attitude or an opinion; if the adjectives helped me visualize a person or situation, I inclined towards that. With the concrete thing, I just looked at the adjectives briefly and thought there's nothing hugely descriptive—like if it was fragrant and aromatic, it was really hard to make that concrete for me. That would give me a feeling of a nice conversation or relationship, and immediately that would become more of an abstract thing for me.
I see.
Yeah, maybe if I couldn't immediately fit something into a concrete category, I'd just consider it abstract as the second part, no matter what the two items at the bottom were.

That's really interesting. So have I understood right that as you moved through it, you were choosing consideration or attitude not so much because of what those words bring, but because the adjectives speak more to an abstract concept?
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
That's really interesting.

Yeah, and I think because abstract things are abstract in nature, you can associate them with lots of different things—you can sort of twist meanings to make them fit. So 'aromatic' doesn't really mean anything as an opinion, but you could associate it with someone having nice opinions or considerations, whereas it's quite hard to fit that into a boomerang.
Yeah, yeah.

Yeah, that's really interesting. A lot of people have said boomerang is a particularly affecting item in the set—lots of people have said they just couldn't get on with boomerang, couldn't do anything with it, which is really interesting.
Yeah.

Because all three of the concrete items were chosen through the same process, but it's really interesting that there's a unique effect happening around boomerang. We'll have to look at the data to try and understand that, but that's another interesting thing.
No, I do agree with that comment actually. I think out of all the items, I probably associated anything with boomerang a lot less.
I wonder why that is.

I think maybe if there was a similar adjective I might have paired it, but I couldn't imagine a smooth or rough edge. For those items it was a bit more visual, as opposed to creative abstracting. If it was a child's cartoon I might be able to have a perfumed boomerang or something, but it was less realistic to me than imagining someone having an aromatic opinion about something.

Yeah, that's really interesting. Because when you make a choice in the experiment, the two adjectives at the top function as a sort of prime—they steer you towards thinking about different senses. But when you make your choice, the complete construction becomes a metaphor either one way or the other. Did you feel like you were creating metaphors or creating something like a poetic unit?

Yeah, I think so, especially with the more abstract ones like opinion. In the back of my head I was very briefly imagining a conversation that was rough and smelly, or a person who was very considerate in a fragrant kind of way. I could sort of see that in the back of my head. I don't know if I was trying to justify an association I wasn't used to, but I could build something and feel there might be a way a conversation could be described as such, even though it's not what you might usually see. So I guess in that sense it is sort of creative.
Brilliant, thank you so much. Is there anything about anything we've done today that we haven't talked about that you would like to talk about?
I'm interested in how the first two exercises linked.
Oh sure.
Yeah.

They're all subtasks from an assessment called the cognitive linguistic quick test. It's used as a screening test designed for everyone, but it has particular tasks that are helpful for indicating whether someone might have a language difficulty. Because we're doing research with people who have a diagnosis of schizophrenia and people who don't, and some people with that diagnosis can sometimes develop language difficulties in relation to it, we use these language cognition subtests to give everyone a score. Then we make sure that when we're comparing data across groups, we're comparing people with the same level on these subtests.
Mm.
Just to rule out any difference in language ability.
Mm.
Just to make sure that the comparisons we make are actually because of the test and not because of differences.
yeah
And that's the only reason we do it. If you like, we can talk about any aspect of it, or if you have any questions.
Yeah, I don't know. You said everybody always does better than they think. Do people always think they didn't find as many M words?
Yeah, yeah.
Or animals, they...
Yeah, so people...
What's the average?

People tend to walk away after coming up with about thirty words and think it was terrible and they're really bad at it. But thirty is actually—incidentally, you gave thirty responses for animals. I think people always produce fewer M words because it's a completely different cognitive process.
mm
But you produced twenty-one M words, and the score you got for that one was the top score.
oh
The overall levels are between one and nine, and you got a nine. That's what I mean—people think because it's difficult...
yeah
They think, 'Oh, I must have done...' But no, that just means what we'll do with your data is compare it with someone who has a diagnosis of schizophrenia but whose language is pretty much preserved.
So those two measures are a measure of language ability?
They're really only measures of performance on those particular tasks, because the actual assessment...
OK
...is done as a battery of ten assessments, and...
mhm

Because we don't do all ten, we couldn't actually generate an accurate measure of language cognition. So these really only allow for a numerical value in the specific context of that specific task, which is enough for matching.
mm
But it wouldn't be enough for doing an analysis on a...
Like a linguistics type of thing.
Yeah, any deeper level than just matching.

So with schizophrenia, does it affect their... I have no idea, I haven't read up about schizophrenia or anything, but to some extent does it affect their language? I assume that's why you're doing it, particularly around creative writing.

Yes, it's a very interesting and unique set of symptoms in schizophrenia. You see very similar symptoms in other clinical pictures, and psychosis isn't exclusive to it. Psychosis can appear in a few other places as well; for example, some people can get Lyme disease and have a psychosis related to that.
Mm.

The psychosis spectrum is really interesting and kind of separate, but there are also overlaps. In schizophrenia, the current thinking around symptoms is that you have two sets: positive symptoms, which kind of add things, like hearing things that might not necessarily be there—so it adds the perception of hearing something—and then you have the negative symptoms, which kind of take stuff away. People tend to say less if they have lots of negative symptoms.
Mm.

Their movement also tends to become less pronounced, that sort of thing. In the negative symptom area, language can be affected. Things like words per sentence can go down, vocabulary can shrink a bit, and lots of other things can happen.
So, regarding the last test we did, are you expecting that people find it harder to make an association, or what kind of things are you looking out for?
My hope is that they will actually find it easier, because...
Ah.

The argument, or the idea I'm putting forward, is that there's something called formal thought disorder, which we don't really know very much about. It's currently described in very vague terms because it's understood vaguely. One of the things about formal thought disorder is that it's been likened to poetic language. Some people who experience formal thought disorder—not everybody with a diagnosis of schizophrenia experiences it—but when people do, their language becomes very abstract.
OK.
So I'm hoping that what we'll see is that people in the schizophrenia group will show a lot more comfort with going both ways.
OK.
Whereas that would offer a potential explanation for why the language does take an abstract form, because the experiment is based on...
Oh, just bear with me a second, sorry.

No, no, it's OK. The experiment is based, or the items are constructed, on a few things we know about cognition and adjectives. The idea is that if we see group differences on this experiment, we can start asking some questions about whether these cognitive principles around adjectives might be involved in formal thought disorder. It's all very tentative and exploratory, but it might be a step toward explaining a piece of how language changes in schizophrenia.
Mm.
Fingers crossed.
Yeah, all the best with it. Have you reached your sample size?
Erm...
Or is it still a way off?
Oh, sorry, the connection skipped a bit.
Oh, sorry, I was just asking if you're getting close to reaching the sample size you want.
Yeah, thank you, thankfully.

Due to the ability to do it remotely, because of everything that's happened lately, but the program the experiment was designed in—the remote version wasn't available until June of this year, so I only found out in June.
Oh, wow.

messages.content: So there's only one question for this interview, and that was: how was the experiment?

It was really interesting, it was fun. I think, obviously this would be the case with everyone participating, but while you're doing it you're very aware of wondering why you're doing it. Particularly with the word task, as my job is kind of words, I am inclined to overthink that sort of thing.

Because you mentioned part of speech and then I thought, okay, you work with language. That doesn't affect the results, but it provides interesting context when we talk about it in the interview. Do you mind telling me a little bit more about that? That's really interesting.

I found it perhaps more difficult than I should have done because I don't like putting words together that don't fit together naturally, grammatically. I don't like having to make a choice between a salty edge and a salty opinion. So my responses perhaps weren't as instinctive as they might have been because I was working on a process of least bad association.
I see.
A least bad association rather than good. And for some reason I took against 'boomerang' and I was aware that I was overthinking that, worrying whether I was giving boomerang a fair chance.

That's really interesting because the actual task has no real correct or incorrect answer. But one of the things that comes through the interviews is people saying that certain items just feel wrong, certain items just feel less preferable than others. I wonder why that is. Were there certain items that really stood out for you?
Yeah.

That's really interesting because the actual task has no real correct or incorrect answer. But one of the things that comes through the interviews is people saying that certain items just feel wrong, certain items just feel less preferable than others. I wonder why that is. Were there certain items that really stood out for you?

Well, I think because the practice ones didn't include 'boomerang'. When I'd been overthinking the practice ones with more nebulous concepts like 'edge' and 'opinion', I had worked my way round to thinking how the adjectives could apply to them. So when I got into the test and 'boomerang' came along, I was worrying about whether I was being valid because they weren't instinctive responses. I worked my way round to a sharpener potentially being a person or a drink or something, and therefore more things could apply to it, whereas a boomerang is just a boomerang, so nebulous adjectives can't apply to it. Whereas with 'opinion' and 'consideration' it got easier, because as soon as I had thought my way to there being a smoothed consideration, then whenever I saw 'smoothed' and 'consideration' I had already said, yep, those two are allowed together.
I see. So am I right in thinking that as you moved through the experiment you developed a rule set for the items?
Definitely, yes.
I see, that's really interesting.
Is that not a good thing? And then I was worrying that that was a bad thing for your experiment.

No, not at all. What the experiment really does is we've taken a few things that we know about cognition in language that seem to apply to adjectives and we've arranged them with certain types of noun in order to create a choice situation where, after you've seen two adjectives that come from different sensory modalities as a pairing, do you opt for a concrete or an abstract noun? What we're seeing is that there is a preference emerging. What people are talking about in the interviews touches on what you're talking about. It doesn't necessarily mean there's a universal pattern or that everybody is using the same pattern.
Oh.

What we're seeing is that there is a preference emerging. What people are talking about in the interviews touches on what you're talking about. It doesn't necessarily mean there's a universal pattern or that everybody is using the same pattern.
Yeah.
But these items tend to be giving people the sense that they need to be looking for and establishing a pattern, which is a very welcome finding but not necessarily one that we were predicting.
Right, yeah.
Which is a very welcome finding but not necessarily one that we were predicting.
Right, yeah.
Which is really interesting. So when you were moving through, I'm really interested in this idea of developing the rule set. How did that come about for you?

Well, I think it came about in the practising. I think there were only abstract nouns in the practising, so having spoken to you I had to think out a way whereby I could happily, within myself, fit the adjective with the noun. Not necessarily as a part of speech, but through a rapid process of going, well, you could say someone had a salty opinion if it was a little bit out of the ordinary. I don't suppose I was thinking of salty in a sensory sense but more in the sense of a salty story or something like that.
Yeah.

So, having agreed with myself that a certain adjective could be used in a certain way and applied to that noun, it became easier afterwards. I feel that using two adjectives can sometimes be a bit superfluous, like a literary flourish. So if you were saying someone had a salty opinion, you could also say it was a smelly one, having already agreed that it could be salty.
Yeah.

Whereas with the boomerang, which as far as I know has just one meaning, there were very few adjectives I could apply. I was aware I just couldn't apply any nebulous adjectives to it. I mean, it could just about have been salty, but then I had to go through a whole process of thinking it would have had to have dropped in the sea first. I felt bad because I missed the opportunity for a salty, smelly boomerang, which was its one chance, and then I'd already clicked on the other one because I'd seen the word 'opinion'.

And that's one of the things that's so interesting about how people interact with the experiment. What's coming through in the interviews is that in the early questions there is a kind of 'how am I going to make sense of this' process.
Mm.
Throughout this, and then after a few items people determine a way to do that. Did you find different words, say, because we have some taste and smell words in there and some sight and sound ones?
Ah, I didn't even realise that actually. That didn't even register with me as we were going along.
Oh, OK. Were some items more memorable than others, or did you find aspects of the experiment stood out?

Actually, I tell a lie. The only time I was aware of it being sensory was when it was 'edge', because I had somehow associated that with a drink. You could say it had a bit of a salty edge to it. Now I think about it, that was very sensory. That would be how I established whether I felt adjectives could go with the word 'edge'. No, now I'm thinking about it more, 'smoothed' was sensory too. Yes, I was definitely more ready to apply 'salty', 'sour', and 'smoothed' to 'edge' and 'sharpener' than any of the other adjectives, and I think that was because I had conceived them perhaps as slightly more sensory nouns.

I see, that's very interesting. The noun choices, as well as being literal and abstract, the literal nouns are also semantically bound to the adjectives. By which I mean we only put literal nouns in the set that were also classified by a semantic tagger as being related to the sensory concepts in the adjectives.
Oh, right.

So on the literal item front, those items are actually tied semantically to the adjectives, whereas the abstract ones aren't. It's really interesting that for those senses, it sounds like the semantic tie was important in your decision-making process.
Mm.
Which is a very linguistic thing to do, if you work with language.
Yeah, yeah.
And...

But is 'edge' enough of a non-abstract noun to be the other non-abstract noun? Or was 'edge' specifically decided on because it is halfway between abstract and not? I mean, a boomerang is absolutely a boomerang, whereas if someone's got an edge to them, I would have thought that was as abstract as an opinion.

Yeah, so this is where the experiment has a set of effects. Because you're working with metaphor primes in the adjective position. If we look at the two adjectives at the top of the screen and the two noun choices underneath, the adjectives are really performing the function of a paired adjective prime, implying they will modify the same noun.
Yeah.

As a paired adjective construction modifying just one of the two nouns. And so by being asked to do that with sensory adjectives that also muddle senses, there is probably an artefact in the experiment where the line between literal and abstract sort of disappears.
Mm.

Because in both cases the choices are being asked to form a metaphor. So even though the noun can be said to be literal, as soon as it's a choice and paired with those adjectives, it becomes the target domain of the metaphor you create when you click. And then the adjectives become the source domain. So you're mapping the paired adjectives as a synaesthesia source domain onto one of the two targets. There's definitely an argument to be made that as soon as a literal or concrete noun becomes the target in a synaesthesia metaphor, it becomes abstract.
Ah.

And then the adjectives become the source domain so you're mapping the paired adjectives as a source domain as a synaesthesia source domain onto one of the two targets and there is there's definitely an argument to be to be made that as soon as a literal noun or a concrete you know noun becomes the target in a synaesthesia metaphor then it becomes abstract.
Wow.
So it's hard to know where the line is, you know?
Yes, yeah.

And this is part of the discussion about the experiment and language experiments generally—how do you actually make these decisions? I mean, we used a semantic tagger from corpus linguistics to try to take the human element out of the decision-making process.
Yeah.
And say, well, this is what the semantic classifier calls a concrete noun and this is what it calls an abstract noun.
Yeah.
But language is a hard thing to do experiments on.
Yeah.
Because they change and things.
Yeah, no, it's really interesting. When will you have written everything up? Is this a very long-term project, or will it be?
It's probably going to be a while before the whole thesis is done, but I'm hoping—
Yeah.
—to write up and share the results of the experiment quite soon, so I'm very happy to share them if—
Oh, that would be lovely, yeah. That would be really interesting, thank you.
Yeah, happy to. I'll make a note, if that's alright.
Yeah.
That will involve holding onto your email address for a little bit, if that's OK.
That's fine.
So, results—is there anything we haven't talked about regarding the experiment that you'd like to discuss?
No, I don't think so. Well, I mean, if you're able to say, I'm interested to know why—what the different tasks meant. But it—
Sure, yeah.
I mean, no, not what they meant—what they're used for, what you're looking at.
Sure. So, at its core, the task is a test of—there's an expression I heard someone say once, that proofreading is editing in a broom cupboard.

And this task is creativity in a broom cupboard in the same way. So the task is really measuring a very specific type of creative judgment—what kind of metaphor you create—with very strict linguistic parameters. You only have certain types of adjectives, certain types of nouns, and they appear in certain orders for certain people in the experiment, different orders for different people. So it's really a creativity measure, but there are no right answers. It's more about seeing if there are differences between groups of people.
Mm.

One thing emerging from the post-task discussions is that people in certain groups seem to be developing their own rulesets for navigating the task, and those rulesets are starting to look group-specific.
mm

That's what we were looking to see. The exact nature of what different groups do is still being examined in the data. The cognitive assessment is just for matching—we're not analyzing it, just ensuring that when we compare experimental data from someone in the schizophrenia group, we're matching them with someone who performed similarly on the assessments.
Oh, right, that's interesting, yeah.
Just so we can rule out the role of linguistic ability.
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
And the interview is looking not only at the content of what we're talking about but also the grammatical structure of natural speech.
mm
And comparing differences across groups there. So there are three very different elements being looked at, and it will all come together.
yeah
But yeah, yeah.
Fascinating. Great, well thank you, that was fun.
Oh thank you. I'll stop the recording now and then let you know what happens next with the debrief sheet and things like that.

messages.content: OK, so the one question for the interview is how was the experiment.
Yeah, it was kind of weird. It was absolutely fine, but just a bit weird. I don't really know how else to explain it.
No, no, that's OK.
Like I kept...
I mean, that's really interesting.

I kept thinking all throughout, have I missed something? Was there a connection there that I was supposed to be picking up? But the words were kind of repeated in very random orders, and we were getting the same words and different choices. It was just... yeah.
That's really interesting. That weirdness, what did it feel like?

I think for me, I clearly wasn't as concerned as I possibly should have been, because I could have asked if I'd actually missed an instruction. But I was 99% certain I didn't miss any, so I just went with it. It was actually quite uncomfortable for me because I like knowing what I'm supposed to be doing.
I see, I see.

I'm very much—you've probably got it from the initial assessment—I like to, it's not so much I like to get things right, though that's true, but when I'm doing something I give it my all even if I'm not amazing at it. With the questions at the start, like name some animals, I know animals, and it's that pressure of being put on the spot but you know you can answer. Whereas this was very abstract, very much I don't know what I'm supposed to be doing really.

Yeah, I was about to say before we started the interview, but I wasn't sure if it was something you wanted to hear. While you were doing the experiment I scored the assessment, and you got full marks for everything. You're in the top—you put the scores together and get categories like levels 1 to 9.
OK.
And you're in 9 for all three tasks, so you got the highest category scores for the assessment. So if that is helpful or nice to know...

It's good to know, because as I say, I do like to get things right. When I try something and I think I've done—I've done things like quizzes where you have your specialist subjects, but when it's something this random, I don't get asked words beginning with M and put on the spot every day. So I kind of feel like, yeah, OK, yay, I'd sort of achieved something there. And then it was just that complete flip of I don't know what I'm doing here.
I see. So the stuff at the beginning, they're three subtasks from something called a cognitive linguistic quick test.
OK.

They measure things like language, memory, executive functions, attention. It just gives us some scores to make sure when we do the group comparisons we're ruling out the effect of, say, if we ran an analysis and had some really significant differences but realised it was because one person in one group was getting 9s and one person in the other group was getting 3s.
Yeah.

That would probably be the reason why the results were different and not what we're looking for in terms of the purpose of the experiment. There is one, but there's no right answer. There's an expression that proofreading is editing in a broom cupboard—a very restricted type of editing. This task is like creativity in a broom cupboard. The choices are between making one creative choice or another, but the constraints are very strict, so you only have certain words to do it with. It's like being given four blocks of Lego and being told to make something.
Yeah.

There are only a certain number of things you can make, but we're still interested in what people make with those four blocks. There's no right answer. So, thinking about the weirdness, was that weirdness there for all of the items or some?
Some more than others, because with some of them I was sort of drawn to one option more than the other.
Oh, OK.

I don't know, maybe it was a kind of word association thing. There was something in the back of my head drawing me to one more than the other. But then the word 'boomerang' appeared quite a lot, and I was like, there's really not much of a connection here that I can go with for either of them. So a lot of the time, I think I started off trying to choose not so much what I thought was right, but more what I felt was right. Then as it went on and I was getting words like 'boomerang' or 'sharpener' coming up, which to me had really no connection, I was more often choosing the other one because that had no connection. So I think I changed my approach to it.
I see.

Not for everything, but when certain ones came up I thought, no, I have no connection with that at all, so I'll go with the other one instead of the one I did connect with. It was a bit of a change in approach.
Yeah, and did that happen quite early on in the items or later?
I'd say, I can't be exact, but probably about halfway through.
Oh, OK.

I was trying not to second-guess myself, in the sense that I wasn't guessing in the first place. I was trying to go with my instinct first of all. Then it got to the point where I was thinking, have I missed something? Is there something else here? I felt more comfortable when I switched to the other approach of let's not go with the one I don't connect with, rather than let's go with the one I connect with more. I felt a bit more comfortable. I'd say probably about halfway through, ish.

I see, that's really interesting. Because in both cases, regardless of the word you choose, you're being asked throughout the experiment to make metaphors. But the word you choose determines whether that metaphor is about a literal or an abstract object.
OK.

And that's one of the things the experiment is really interested in: do people choose to make their metaphors out of concrete things or abstract things like ideas, opinions, attitudes, or tangible objects? And are there any differences in groups for those choices? So that's what the experiment is measuring.
Yeah.
But we obviously, I obviously wait until the end to tell people this, because if I tell them before then that will affect their selections.
Yeah.

But yeah, it's like a metaphor creation task. And I wonder if that feeling of weirdness was related to—well, would you say it was more about the choices or more about the words that came up on the top?
I think it was—that's a good question actually—it was more about the choices.
I see.
It was more about the choices, yeah.
Oh, OK. And the words at the top, was that less uncomfortable in terms of the feeling you got from those words?

Yeah, I mean, I found those words—it was a bit odd because occasionally I'd look at them and think, I've got nothing here, I've just got nothing together with that. So there were almost four different scenarios: sometimes the top words went together and I could easily pick one of the two options; then you'd have the top words going together but neither option appealed to me; then the top words not really fitting together and neither option appealing; and the top words not really fitting together where it wasn't that one was better, it was basically that one option was worse than the other, so I went for the better one, if that makes sense.
I see, yeah, yeah.
But that wasn't really occurring to me at the time, it's sort of occurring to me now looking back on it.
Yeah, and what you say there with the four options sounds a lot like the four sublists within the item list. So there are four different—
Yeah.

—types of item: adjectives that do go together better than others, adjectives that kind of clash, and nouns that go with the adjectives and nouns that don't go with the adjectives. So the fact that that's come out of your experience is really interesting, because that's part of the experimental design to make sure we don't have a list that's influencing people to make a certain choice because of the way the list is. But it's really interesting that as you're going through, you're getting that sense that the items are categorized. That's really interesting.

Yeah, I think at first when you're seeing the words repeated but not necessarily exactly the same, there's that possibility in your head of going, well, this is just really random words coming up. And you know, obviously it's got a basis in the research, so it's not going to be completely random, there's going to be a process to it. But again, I don't think I dissected it while I was doing it; it was more now I'm looking back and going, that's probably why I picked that. And I think as well, for me, I've never classed myself as a creative person. I'm very much a tangible person, certainly in terms of ideas and the abstract and stuff like that. So that'd be quite interesting as to what side I came down on that.
Yeah, that's really interesting. And yeah, well, what I can do is, if people would like, I can send them the results.
Oh, that'd be great.
of the overall experiment
yeah

but it's also possible, if you're interested, I can make you a graph of which side you came down on personally, like your results. But that would involve keeping your email address to send it to you, if that's OK.
that's absolutely fine, yeah
but yeah, I'll send you a graph of which choices you made more of, literal or
yeah
abstract
I'd be quite interested in that, actually
and the results as well
yeah
but yeah, no, that's—is there anything you'd like to talk about regarding the experiment that we haven't talked about?
I don't think so. I mean, it was good to get that understanding. I think if I'd just gone away after it, I'd have been going, what on earth was that?
yeah
and that weirdness doesn't really seem as weird anymore. I think now that I've recognized what I did and why I made those choices, it's a lot less weird.
that's good, that's good
yeah

because walking away from participation in something like this without getting any information about what you did—I don't think that's a very nice experience. And that's one of the reasons I really like including in this conversation a bit of an explanation about what the experiment is actually doing, because then, like you say, you have a bit more to take away and go, oh right.
yeah
so that's why I was—that's why
yeah
that felt the way it felt. But I hope it wasn't too uncomfortable.
I do like stuff like this, because I find I learn a little bit more about myself each time I do something like this.
I see, yeah
which is quite good
yeah

I'm not a reflective person. I actually took part in a study a couple of months ago where I did a five-minute video diary every day for two weeks. They gave you prompt questions, but you could talk about whatever you liked. I've never kept a diary in my life.
I see.

But doing this—you could do it at any time during the day, I think between eleven in the morning and eleven at night—the amount I learned about myself just from doing that for two weeks was incredible.
Yeah.
It's brilliant.
Yeah, especially.
So yeah, I love stuff like this.
I'm pleased. Was it sort of fun to take part in?
Yeah.
Even though at times it was uncomfortable with the experiment?

Yeah, absolutely. I think that's part of it for me. If you only stick with what you're comfortable with and what you already know, you might build on your skills in those areas, but you're not going to expand what you know.
Yeah.

Which isn't for everyone, but it is for me. That's the kind of thing I quite like to do. I'm not saying I want to go out and learn how to crochet or something, but little things like this can help develop you.
Oh yeah.
And for me, one of the big things I've always wanted to work on is my understanding of myself in terms of reflection, because it's not something I'm good at.
Well, I don't get that sense from you, because this whole discussion, it seems to me like you've been reflecting.
I think it's not something I'm good at on my own, maybe.
Oh, OK.

I think if you put me in a position like this, where I'm directly asked that question—even in the context of 'how did you find that?' or in the video diary example—whereas if I just tried to do something like that for myself, I'd either get bored or it would take a long time to get into the habit of sitting there and thinking, 'Actually, how was my day?'
Yeah.

So I think I get more of a sense of purpose out of it when I'm doing it for something or for someone else, whereas just for myself maybe I'm not as good. So it's good to know that I can do it, and clearly I can. It's just now finding the impetus, the reason, and the purpose for doing it.
Yeah, but it sounds like—I totally agree that you absolutely can. I think sometimes it's about time as well, isn't it?
Yes.
Like you say, when you're asked and when there's time set aside for it, that creates the space for it. And sometimes if you're really busy, then it's harder.

Yeah, I think that's exactly it. It's like anything: if you really want to do something, you're going to make the time for it. And I think for me, I find that I will make time for things that involve other people more than I'd make time for something just for myself. I mean, we all have our own time, our 'me time' and everything like that. But I think setting aside even just five minutes in a day to do a video diary—I could do that for a research project, but to get it into my head to just do it for myself would take a lot more effort, I think.
I see

But I don't know, that's just a reflection on myself that I know I'd like to work on. Because it's exactly as you say, there's that never-ending list: you've got work, you've got to go shopping, do the housework, make dinner, whatever you have to do throughout a normal day. Trying to fit something into that routine where it won't be seen as a chore—I think that's the key thing.
Mm, yeah.
You don't want to be sitting there thinking, 'Oh, I have to do this today.'
Yeah, they do say that.
So.
That the second you make something an obligation, it becomes so much harder to do it.
Yep.
Erm.
Yeah.
But that's—
But no, this was really fun.
Oh good, I'm really pleased.
This was really fun.
Thank you so much. Shall I stop the recording for the interview? Then I'll just let you know what happens next. There's one last bit of paperwork, but we don't have to fill it in, it's just a—
OK.

case_summary: The participant describes their experience of a metaphor-creation experiment as 'weird' and uncomfortable due to uncertainty about the task's purpose and a perceived lack of clear instructions. They detail their shifting strategy for making choices, moving from instinct to a more deliberate avoidance of disconnected options. The participant reflects on their personality, noting a preference for tangible over abstract thinking, a drive to perform well, and a difficulty with self-reflection unless prompted by an external structure or purpose. The debriefing resolved their initial confusion.
no_delusion_point_reason: The participant's statements describe subjective feelings of confusion, discomfort, and personal cognitive strategies during an ambiguous experimental task. They express uncertainty about the task's purpose ('have I missed something?') and later accept the researcher's explanation, which resolves the 'weirdness'. There is no expression of a fixed, false belief about external reality; the content reflects normal reactions to an ambiguous situation, self-reflection on personality traits, and task-related problem-solving.
